title: Well-Child Care: Growth, Development, Prevention, Family Context
bottomLine: Well-child care is longitudinal surveillance of growth, development, immunization, nutrition, oral health, injury prevention, mental health and family/social context. A single normal milestone screen does not replace ongoing developmental surveillance.
recognize: Growth crossing percentiles, loss of milestones, language delay or caregiver concern can be early signals.
differentiate: Normal developmental variation differs from regression, which is always concerning.
assessment: Plot growth accurately, review feeding, sleep, elimination, milestones, hearing/vision, behaviour, school, immunization, dental care and social determinants.
workup: Use age-appropriate validated developmental screening and targeted hearing/vision/laboratory evaluation based on findings rather than routine broad testing.
management: Provide anticipatory guidance and refer early to developmental, speech-language, audiology or other services when concerns are identified; do not wait for a definitive label before supporting development.
medicationSafety: Use weight-based pediatric dosing and verify concentration for liquid medicines.
counselling: Use strengths-based family-centred language and respect cultural child-rearing practices while addressing safety.
followUp: Reassess concerns on a defined timeline and document referral completion.
examTrap: Telling a parent to wait until school age for a significant language delay because children develop at different rates.
oneLinePearl: Developmental concern deserves early support even before the final diagnosis is known.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society early child development and autism surveillance resources
Rourke Baby Record principles

title: Newborn Jaundice: Plot the Bilirubin Against Age in Hours
bottomLine: Newborn bilirubin risk depends on gestational age, postnatal age in hours and neurotoxicity risk factors. Visible jaundice alone cannot determine treatment; early severe or rapidly rising bilirubin requires urgent evaluation.
recognize: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathologic until assessed; poor feeding and dehydration can worsen bilirubin.
differentiate: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia is common; conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is never physiologic and needs cholestasis evaluation.
assessment: Assess gestational age, age in hours, feeding/weight loss, stool/urine, bruising, blood-group/hemolysis risk, family history and neurologic state.
workup: Measure bilirubin and plot against current CPS treatment thresholds; obtain hemolysis or direct bilirubin studies when indicated.
management: Use feeding support and phototherapy at guideline thresholds; escalate severe cases for intensive phototherapy or exchange-transfusion pathway.
medicationSafety: Do not rely on sunlight as treatment for significant hyperbilirubinemia.
counselling: Teach parents when jaundice or feeding changes require same-day reassessment.
followUp: Discharge follow-up timing depends on bilirubin level relative to treatment threshold, gestational age and feeding risk.
examTrap: Interpreting a bilirubin value without knowing the newborn's age in hours.
oneLinePearl: A newborn bilirubin number has no meaning without age in hours and gestational risk.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society hyperbilirubinemia guideline 2025

title: Newborn Hypoglycemia: Screen the At-Risk Infant, Treat the Symptomatic Infant
bottomLine: Routine glucose screening is for newborns with recognized risk factors, not every healthy infant. Symptomatic or persistently low glucose requires prompt feeding or IV treatment based on severity while identifying the cause.
recognize: Risk includes infants of diabetic mothers, preterm, SGA or LGA infants and some ill newborns; symptoms can include jitteriness, poor feeding, apnea, lethargy or seizure.
differentiate: Jitteriness can be benign or caused by hypocalcemia, withdrawal or neurologic disease; confirm glucose.
assessment: Assess feeding, temperature, gestational age, birthweight percentile, maternal diabetes/medications and clinical symptoms.
workup: Use bedside glucose with laboratory confirmation when clinically necessary; persistent hypoglycemia beyond transitional period needs endocrine/metabolic evaluation.
management: Feed promptly when appropriate, use dextrose gel in eligible asymptomatic cases according to protocol, and IV dextrose for severe/symptomatic hypoglycemia.
medicationSafety: Avoid rapid uncontrolled hyperglycemia during IV correction; calculate neonatal glucose infusion carefully.
counselling: Support breastfeeding while treating hypoglycemia rather than presenting supplementation as feeding failure.
followUp: Ensure persistent hypoglycemia is resolved before discharge and feeding is reliable.
examTrap: Screening every healthy term newborn repeatedly with no risk factor or symptom.
oneLinePearl: Screen risk, treat symptoms, investigate persistence.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society newborn hypoglycemia statement updated 2025

title: Newborn Feeding and Weight Loss: Is Intake Adequate?
bottomLine: Early weight loss must be interpreted with feeding effectiveness, urine/stool output, jaundice and hydration. Excessive loss or poor transfer requires observed feeding and active support, not simply telling a parent to feed more often.
recognize: Delayed lactogenesis, ineffective latch, ankyloglossia in selected cases, prematurity and maternal illness can reduce transfer.
differentiate: Normal early physiologic loss differs from dehydration, hypernatremia or failure to regain weight on an appropriate trajectory.
assessment: Observe a feed, assess latch/swallowing, breast/chest anatomy as relevant, infant oral exam, urine/stool pattern and maternal pain/medications.
workup: Use weight trend and bilirubin; obtain electrolytes when severe dehydration or hypernatremia is suspected.
management: Use skilled lactation support and individualized supplementation when medically indicated while protecting milk supply and feeding goals.
medicationSafety: Do not recommend unsafe herbal galactagogues without evidence/risk review.
counselling: Avoid shame around feeding method; infant hydration and parental goals both matter.
followUp: Reweigh promptly after intervention until trajectory is secure.
examTrap: Assuming frequent time at the breast proves adequate milk transfer.
oneLinePearl: Feeding frequency is not feeding effectiveness.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society newborn nutrition resources
Baby-Friendly Initiative principles

title: Growth Faltering: Intake, Absorption, Demand, or Social Barrier?
bottomLine: Growth faltering is a trajectory problem, not a single small percentile. Verify accurate measurements, assess caloric intake and feeding interaction first, then investigate malabsorption, chronic disease, increased metabolic demand and social determinants based on clues.
recognize: Weight typically falters before length/height in insufficient intake; head growth is usually preserved until severe/prolonged undernutrition.
differentiate: Constitutionally small children follow a consistent curve; crossing percentiles or growth deceleration is more concerning.
assessment: Obtain detailed feeding history, observe mealtime when possible, review stool/vomiting, chronic symptoms, development and food security.
workup: Broad screening labs have low yield without clinical clues; use targeted CBC, celiac, thyroid, inflammatory or other tests as indicated.
management: Increase nutritional density and feeding support, treat disease and connect families to food/income/community resources; hospitalize medically unstable severe malnutrition.
medicationSafety: Avoid appetite stimulants as first-line treatment before cause and feeding environment are understood.
counselling: Avoid blaming caregivers; barriers may be financial, developmental, sensory or medical.
followUp: Track weight velocity and developmental progress frequently until stable.
examTrap: Ordering a massive laboratory panel before verifying measurements and observing feeding.
oneLinePearl: Growth faltering is a curve and a feeding story before it is a lab panel.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society nutrition and community pediatrics resources

title: Croup: Steroid for All, Epinephrine for Significant Stridor
bottomLine: Typical croup is a barky cough with hoarseness and inspiratory stridor. Corticosteroid therapy is the mainstay across severity; nebulized epinephrine is added for moderate or severe respiratory distress and requires observation for recurrence.
recognize: Symptoms often worsen at night and follow a viral prodrome.
differentiate: Drooling, toxic appearance and tripod posture suggest epiglottitis; sudden choking suggests foreign body; high fever with poor appearance can suggest bacterial tracheitis.
assessment: Assess stridor at rest, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, fatigue and ability to drink; minimize agitation.
workup: Routine x-ray and viral testing are not needed in classic croup.
management: Give dexamethasone; use nebulized epinephrine for significant stridor or distress and escalate airway support for impending failure.
medicationSafety: Do not repeatedly agitate a child with unnecessary throat examination or procedures when upper-airway obstruction is possible.
redFlags: Age <6 months or unusually severe/recurrent disease
counselling: Teach parents that cough can persist while breathing danger is defined by stridor at rest and work of breathing.
followUp: Observe after epinephrine long enough to ensure sustained improvement.
examTrap: Ordering neck x-rays for classic croup before giving dexamethasone.
oneLinePearl: Croup is clinical: steroid first; image only when the story is not croup.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society acute croup statement updated 2026

title: Acute Otitis Media: Bulging Membrane, Not a Red Eardrum
bottomLine: AOM requires acute symptoms plus middle-ear effusion and inflammation, typically a bulging tympanic membrane. A red membrane from crying or viral URI alone is not enough for antibiotics.
recognize: Ear pain, fever and irritability are common; otorrhea can reflect perforation.
differentiate: Otitis externa causes canal tenderness; otitis media with effusion lacks acute infection symptoms.
assessment: Use pneumatic otoscopy when possible and assess age, severity, bilateral disease, otorrhea and immune/craniofacial risk.
workup: No routine imaging or cultures for uncomplicated AOM.
management: Provide analgesia and use antibiotics or watchful waiting according to age, severity and diagnostic certainty; amoxicillin is common first-line when antibiotics are indicated.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessarily broad antibiotics and document whether the penicillin allergy is credible.
counselling: Pain control is important even when watchful waiting is chosen.
followUp: Reassess treatment failure or recurrent disease.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics because the tympanic membrane looks red after a child has been crying.
oneLinePearl: AOM is a bulging middle-ear diagnosis, not a redness diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society AOM statement reaffirmed 2024

title: Pediatric Pneumonia: Respiratory Effort and Oxygenation Drive Severity
bottomLine: Community-acquired pneumonia in children is often a clinical diagnosis. Tachypnea, hypoxemia, increased work of breathing, dehydration and age/comorbidity determine severity; routine chest x-ray is not required for every uncomplicated outpatient case.
recognize: Fever, cough, tachypnea and focal crackles or decreased breath sounds can occur.
differentiate: Bronchiolitis in infants is usually viral and diffuse; asthma causes wheeze/airflow obstruction; foreign body may be abrupt and focal.
assessment: Assess oxygenation, work of breathing, hydration, age, immunization and comorbidity.
workup: Use chest radiograph for severe, complicated, unclear or non-improving disease rather than routine uncomplicated cases.
management: Use supportive care for viral disease and narrow first-line antibiotics for likely bacterial pneumonia according to age and immunization; admit hypoxemic, dehydrated or significantly distressed children.
medicationSafety: Avoid cough/cold medicines in young children and avoid broad antibiotic coverage without indication.
counselling: Give return precautions for work of breathing, intake and lethargy.
followUp: Reassess failure to improve within the expected interval.
examTrap: Ordering chest x-ray and broad antibiotics for every febrile child with cough but no respiratory distress or focal findings.
oneLinePearl: In pediatric pneumonia, the child's breathing is more important than the x-ray picture.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society respiratory and antimicrobial stewardship principles

title: Pediatric UTI: Get a Valid Urine Sample Before Antibiotics
bottomLine: In a febrile young child without a source, UTI matters—but diagnosis requires pyuria and a properly collected culture. Bag urine is useful for screening only and should not be used to confirm UTI by culture.
recognize: Infants may have fever, poor feeding or vomiting without urinary symptoms; older children may report dysuria/frequency.
differentiate: Asymptomatic bacteriuria and contaminated specimens should not be labelled UTI.
assessment: Assess age, fever, urinary symptoms, prior UTI/anomaly, hydration and sepsis.
workup: Obtain catheter or clean-catch urine for culture in non-toilet-trained children when UTI is sufficiently likely; urinalysis guides interpretation.
management: Treat febrile UTI with age-appropriate antibiotics and escalate toxic, vomiting or very young infants; imaging is selective rather than automatic after every UTI.
medicationSafety: Choose antibiotics from local pediatric resistance patterns and adjust to culture.
counselling: Teach proper urine collection and return precautions.
followUp: Review culture and stop/change antibiotics when results do not support the initial diagnosis.
examTrap: Diagnosing UTI from a positive bag-urine culture.
oneLinePearl: A contaminated urine sample creates a contaminated diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society pediatric UTI guidance

title: Pediatric Constipation: Withholding, Impaction, and Red Flags
bottomLine: Most childhood constipation is functional and maintained by painful stool withholding. Treat impaction first when present, then use sustained osmotic therapy and toileting routines long enough to break the cycle.
recognize: Large hard stools, painful defecation, stool withholding and fecal soiling are typical.
differentiate: Delayed meconium, severe distension, poor growth, neurologic signs or abnormal anus/spine suggest organic disease.
assessment: Assess stool pattern, pain, withholding, diet, toilet training, medications, growth and neurologic/anorectal red flags.
workup: Routine x-ray and laboratory testing are not needed for typical functional constipation.
management: Disimpact when required, then use polyethylene glycol or another evidence-based maintenance regimen plus scheduled toilet sitting and positive reinforcement.
medicationSafety: Stopping laxative immediately after one normal stool often leads to relapse; prolonged maintenance is commonly required.
counselling: Avoid punishment for stool accidents; encopresis is often overflow, not deliberate behaviour.
followUp: Titrate to regular soft stools and taper only after sustained symptom control.
examTrap: Treating fecal soiling as diarrhea or behavioural defiance without checking for impaction.
oneLinePearl: In constipated children, stool leakage often means the rectum is too full, not too empty.
sourceBasis: Canadian pediatric gastroenterology practice resources

title: Febrile Seizure: Simple Pattern or CNS Infection?
bottomLine: A simple febrile seizure is brief, generalized, occurs once in 24 hours in the typical age range and has full recovery. Complex features, meningismus, persistent altered state or an atypical age require broader evaluation.
recognize: Simple febrile seizures are frightening but generally have a benign neurologic prognosis.
differentiate: Meningitis, encephalitis, epilepsy and metabolic seizures must be considered when the pattern is atypical.
assessment: Assess seizure duration/focality/recurrence, recovery, fever source, immunization, meningismus and development.
workup: Routine EEG, neuroimaging and broad labs are not required after a simple febrile seizure in a well child; investigate the cause of fever appropriately.
management: Stop a prolonged active seizure according to acute seizure protocol; otherwise provide fever comfort care and parent education.
medicationSafety: Antipyretics improve comfort but do not reliably prevent recurrent febrile seizures.
counselling: Teach seizure first aid and recurrence expectations.
followUp: Complex or atypical seizures may require pediatric/neurology follow-up.
examTrap: Ordering CT and EEG routinely after a classic simple febrile seizure in a well child.
oneLinePearl: Simple febrile seizure needs fever-source assessment and reassurance, not a neurologic test battery.
sourceBasis: Canadian pediatric emergency practice resources

title: Kawasaki Disease: Prolonged Fever With Coronary Risk
bottomLine: Prolonged unexplained fever with mucocutaneous inflammation, especially in a young child, should trigger Kawasaki disease assessment because delayed IVIG increases coronary-artery complication risk. Infants can have incomplete presentations.
recognize: Conjunctival injection, oral changes, rash, extremity changes and cervical lymphadenopathy are classic features.
differentiate: Scarlet fever, viral exanthem, toxic shock and MIS-C can overlap.
assessment: Track fever duration, cardiac symptoms, mucocutaneous features, irritability and hydration.
workup: Use inflammatory labs, CBC/chemistry/urinalysis and echocardiography according to current CPS guidance; incomplete disease uses supportive lab/echo criteria.
management: Treat promptly with IVIG and aspirin under pediatric/cardiology guidance; arrange coronary follow-up.
medicationSafety: Aspirin use in Kawasaki disease is a specialist exception to routine pediatric aspirin avoidance.
counselling: Explain why cardiology follow-up continues even after fever resolves.
followUp: Repeat echocardiography according to coronary-risk classification.
examTrap: Excluding Kawasaki disease in an infant because not all five classic clinical features are present.
oneLinePearl: Incomplete Kawasaki disease is especially important in young infants with prolonged fever.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society Kawasaki disease guidance posted 2025

title: Pediatric Head Trauma: Image for Intracranial Risk, Not Reassurance
bottomLine: Most minor pediatric head injuries do not require CT. Use age-validated clinical risk assessment, observe when appropriate and image when intracranial injury risk justifies radiation exposure.
recognize: Vomiting, severe mechanism, altered mental status, signs of skull fracture and age-specific risk features influence management.
differentiate: Concussion can exist with a normal CT; CT is for structural injury, not concussion confirmation.
assessment: Assess GCS/mental status, mechanism, LOC, vomiting, severe headache, scalp/skull findings, seizure, neurologic deficit and safeguarding concerns.
workup: Use validated pediatric head injury rules and clinical observation; avoid skull x-ray as a substitute for indicated CT.
management: Observe low/intermediate-risk children appropriately and transfer/image high-risk injury; treat cervical or multisystem trauma concurrently.
medicationSafety: Avoid sedating medications that obscure evolving neurologic status early after injury when possible.
counselling: Give written concussion and deterioration precautions.
followUp: Use graded return to school/activity for concussion symptoms.
examTrap: Ordering CT solely because a child has a concussion diagnosis.
oneLinePearl: CT answers 'is there structural injury?', not 'is there concussion?'.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society acute head trauma statement 2025

title: Autism and Developmental Delay: Refer for Support While Diagnosis Proceeds
bottomLine: Social-communication differences, restricted or repetitive behaviours, language delay or developmental regression should trigger structured developmental assessment. Early intervention does not need to wait for the final autism diagnostic appointment.
recognize: Reduced joint attention, limited gestures, repetitive behaviours, sensory differences and atypical social reciprocity can be clues.
differentiate: Hearing loss, language disorder, global developmental delay and trauma can overlap or coexist.
assessment: Obtain developmental history across settings, caregiver concerns, regression, hearing/vision, adaptive function and school/daycare reports.
workup: Use validated autism/developmental tools and hearing assessment; genetic/metabolic testing is individualized to phenotype.
management: Refer for diagnostic assessment and immediately connect to speech-language, occupational, developmental and educational supports based on needs.
medicationSafety: Medication treats co-occurring symptoms, not core autism itself; avoid unsupported biomedical therapies.
counselling: Use neurodiversity-affirming, family-centred language and discuss strengths as well as support needs.
followUp: Primary care continues coordination of physical, mental and developmental health after diagnosis.
examTrap: Waiting for a formal autism diagnosis before referring a toddler with clear language and social-communication delay to early intervention.
oneLinePearl: Support the developmental need now; the diagnostic label can follow.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society autism early detection and post-diagnostic management guidance

title: Pediatric AKI: Small Creatinine Changes Matter
bottomLine: Acute kidney injury in children can be missed because creatinine is low at baseline. Track change from baseline and urine output, identify perfusion, intrinsic renal and obstructive causes, and document follow-up because childhood AKI increases later CKD and hypertension risk.
recognize: Dehydration, sepsis, nephrotoxins, glomerulonephritis and obstruction are important causes.
differentiate: A 'normal-range' creatinine can still represent a major rise for a small child.
assessment: Assess fluid losses/intake, weight, urine output, nephrotoxic medications, BP, edema and systemic renal features.
workup: Use creatinine trend, electrolytes, urinalysis, urine protein and ultrasound when obstruction is possible; expand workup according to cause.
management: Restore perfusion when depleted, stop nephrotoxins, correct dangerous electrolytes and involve nephrology for severe, unclear or persistent AKI.
medicationSafety: Renally clear or nephrotoxic pediatric drugs require dose and monitoring adjustment during AKI.
counselling: Explain avoidance of dehydration/nephrotoxins during recovery.
followUp: Document the AKI episode and arrange BP, renal function and urine follow-up after discharge.
examTrap: Calling a child's creatinine normal because it falls within an adult laboratory reference range despite doubling from baseline.
oneLinePearl: In children, creatinine trajectory matters more than the adult reference box.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society pediatric AKI statement 2025

title: Adolescent Care: Confidentiality, Capacity, Safety, and Time Alone
bottomLine: Adolescents need developmentally appropriate confidential care, including private time when safe. Capacity is decision-specific rather than determined only by age, and confidentiality has limits when serious safety or mandatory-reporting concerns exist.
recognize: Youth may disclose sexual health, substance use, mental health or abuse only when privacy is explained clearly.
differentiate: Parental disagreement does not automatically mean a capable adolescent cannot consent; exact legal rules vary by province/territory.
assessment: Explain confidentiality and its limits before sensitive questions; assess capacity, coercion, safety, sexual health, substances, mood and supports.
workup: No test replaces a confidential psychosocial interview.
management: Provide confidential evidence-based care within provincial law and local policy; involve trusted adults when the adolescent agrees or when safety/legal obligations require it.
medicationSafety: Consider privacy in pharmacy, portal and billing communications so treatment is not inadvertently disclosed.
redFlags: Inability to understand a high-risk decision
counselling: Tell both youth and caregivers that private adolescent time is routine practice, not a sign of mistrust.
followUp: Document consent/capacity and confidentiality decisions without unnecessary sensitive detail.
examTrap: Refusing contraception or STI care solely because a capable adolescent arrived without a parent.
oneLinePearl: Adolescent consent is about capacity and law, not a birthday alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society adolescent health resources
provincial consent law

title: Child Maltreatment: Safety Before Certainty
bottomLine: When history, injury pattern, behaviour or caregiver interaction raises concern for abuse or neglect, the clinician's job is to protect the child and report according to provincial law—not to prove abuse beyond doubt before acting.
recognize: Injuries inconsistent with development or history, patterned bruises/burns, multiple injury ages, sentinel injuries in nonmobile infants and delayed care are concerning.
differentiate: Medical mimics such as bleeding disorders or bone disease should be considered without using them to postpone immediate safety action.
assessment: Obtain developmentally appropriate history separately when possible, perform full exam, assess siblings and immediate safety, and document objective findings precisely.
workup: Use child-maltreatment team protocols for skeletal survey, neuroimaging, labs or STI testing based on age and injury pattern.
management: Treat injuries, consult child-protection expertise and report reasonable suspicion to the appropriate child-welfare authority under local law.
medicationSafety: Provide necessary analgesia; pain treatment does not compromise forensic assessment.
counselling: Avoid accusatory confrontation that increases risk or contaminates the child's account.
followUp: Coordinate medical, psychosocial and safety follow-up.
examTrap: Waiting until you are certain who caused an injury before making a mandated child-protection report.
oneLinePearl: Safeguarding thresholds are about reasonable concern, not courtroom proof.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society maltreatment resources
provincial child-protection law

title: Pediatric Obesity: Growth, Health, and Stigma-Free Treatment
bottomLine: Pediatric obesity care assesses growth trajectory, metabolic and mechanical complications, sleep, mental health, medications and family context without shame. Treatment intensity should match severity and complications, and should not create eating-disorder harm.
recognize: Hypertension, dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes, MASLD, OSA, orthopedic pain and psychosocial distress can occur.
differentiate: Endocrine causes of weight gain are uncommon and usually have poor linear growth or other disease-specific features.
assessment: Plot BMI-for-age and growth, assess sleep, diet access, activity, medications, puberty, eating-disorder symptoms, bullying and family history.
workup: Screen metabolic comorbidity according to age/severity/risk; do not order endocrine panels solely because weight is high if linear growth is normal.
management: Use family-centred behavioural and nutritional support; refer severe or complicated disease for multidisciplinary pharmacologic or surgical obesity treatment when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Anti-obesity medications in youth require age-specific Canadian authorization/guidance and mental-health/eating-disorder assessment.
redFlags: Rapid weight change with poor height growth
counselling: Focus on health, function and sustainable family changes rather than stigmatizing weight goals.
followUp: Track cardiometabolic outcomes, growth and wellbeing.
examTrap: Ordering cortisol testing for every child with obesity despite normal height velocity and no Cushing features.
oneLinePearl: Most pediatric obesity is not endocrine; poor linear growth is the endocrine clue.
sourceBasis: Obesity Canada pediatric guidance
Canadian Paediatric Society community pediatrics resources
